net-troubleshoot.heading: Documenting as you go
body: The last step of the method, documenting findings, actions and outcomes, is the one most often skipped and the one that pays back most. A good ticket note records the symptom in the user's words, what you tested and what each test showed, the change you made, and how you confirmed the fix. When the same fault returns next month, that note turns an hour of rediscovery into five minutes.

Documentation also protects you during the fix. Before changing a configuration, save the current one (copy running-config, export the firewall policy) so you can roll back. Change one thing at a time and re-test after each change; if you change three settings at once and the problem goes away, you do not know which one fixed it, or whether the other two broke something else.

rt-static.heading: When static routing is the right choice
body: Static routes are not a beginner's shortcut; they are the correct design in several places. A stub network with a single exit, such as a branch office with one link to headquarters, needs only a default route: there is no alternative path for a protocol to discover. Static routes are also predictable, use no CPU or bandwidth for protocol updates, and cannot be manipulated by a rogue device sending forged routing updates.

Their weakness is that they do not react. If the next hop fails but the interface stays up, the router keeps sending traffic into a black hole. Pair important static routes with a tracking mechanism (an IP SLA probe that removes the route when the next hop stops answering) or a floating static backup, and document every static route, because nobody remembers why a route to 10.99.0.0/16 exists three years later.

rt-rip.heading: Why RIP survives, and where you will meet it
body: RIP's limits are severe: a 15-hop maximum, a hop-count metric that ignores bandwidth, and convergence measured in minutes. Modern enterprise networks use OSPF, EIGRP or IS-IS instead. RIP still appears in small legacy networks, in some embedded and industrial devices, and on certification exams, because it is the clearest example of how distance-vector routing works and fails.

If you inherit a RIP network, harden it before replacing it: run RIPv2 (RIPv1 has no authentication and no subnet masks), enable MD5 or keyed authentication on every interface, and make interfaces that face hosts passive so the router does not advertise to, or accept updates from, user segments. Then plan the migration to a link-state protocol.

rt-eigrp.heading: Watching DUAL work
body: The topology table is where EIGRP's speed comes from. `show ip eigrp topology` lists, for each prefix, the successor and any feasible successors with their feasible distance (FD) and reported distance (RD). A route is a feasible successor only if its RD is lower than the current FD, which guarantees the path is loop-free. When the successor fails, a feasible successor is installed immediately, with no queries sent.

If no feasible successor exists, the route goes active and the router queries its neighbours. In a large network those queries can spread widely, and a router that never gets an answer leaves the route stuck-in-active, resetting the neighbour that failed to reply. Summarising routes and configuring stub routers bounds the query scope, which is why the scaling section stresses them.

rt-isis.heading: Operating IS-IS day to day
body: The commands mirror OSPF's. `show isis neighbors` confirms adjacencies and their level (L1, L2 or L1L2); `show isis database` lists the link-state PDUs each router holds, which should be identical across routers in the same level; and `show ip route isis` shows what IS-IS actually installed. A missing adjacency is usually a mismatched level, mismatched area on an L1 link, mismatched MTU or authentication, or an interface where IS-IS is not enabled.

Because IS-IS carries its information in TLVs rather than fixed packet formats, it was extended for IPv6 without a new protocol version and is the usual base for segment routing and traffic engineering in provider networks. Enable authentication for both hellos and LSPs; without it a device on the link can form an adjacency and inject routes.

rt-redistribution.heading: A worked mutual-redistribution design
body: Consider two routers, R1 and R2, each connected to an OSPF domain and an EIGRP domain and redistributing in both directions. Without controls, a route from EIGRP enters OSPF at R1, crosses OSPF to R2, and is redistributed back into EIGRP, sometimes with a better metric than the original. Traffic then loops or takes the long way.

The standard fix is tagging. When R1 and R2 redistribute EIGRP into OSPF they set tag 100; when redistributing OSPF into EIGRP they deny anything carrying tag 100, and the reverse for tag 200. Also set an explicit seed metric for every redistribution, filter with prefix lists so only intended networks cross, and verify on both routers with `show ip route` that each prefix is learned from its native protocol.

rt-routing-security.heading: A hardening checklist for routers
body: Protect the control plane first. Authenticate every routing adjacency (OSPF and IS-IS authentication, BGP TCP-AO or MD5 passwords), make interfaces facing users passive so they never form adjacencies, and use control-plane policing to rate-limit traffic aimed at the router itself. For BGP, also set maximum-prefix limits and the GTSM TTL check (RFC 5082) so a session cannot be spoofed from far away.

Then protect what the router accepts and announces. Filter inbound routes with prefix lists, drop bogons and your own prefixes arriving from outside, validate origins with RPKI, and filter outbound so you only announce your own space; that last rule is what prevents you from causing a route leak. Finally, manage the device over SSH from a management network only, with AAA and logging to a SIEM.

rt-routing-troubleshooting.heading: A worked fault: the missing route
body: Users in 10.20.0.0/24 cannot reach a server in 10.50.0.0/24. On the users' gateway, `show ip route 10.50.0.5` returns nothing, so the problem is the control plane, not the data path. `show ip ospf neighbor` shows the neighbour toward the server stuck in EXSTART. That state usually means an MTU mismatch: the two sides disagree on interface MTU, so database description packets are rejected.

`show interface` confirms one side at 1500 and the other at 9000 after a recent change. Matching the MTU brings the adjacency to FULL, and the route appears. The lesson is to follow the order: table, then adjacency, then path. Each step narrows the fault, and the adjacency state alone often names the cause.

cy-threat-actors.heading: Turning actor knowledge into defence
body: Knowing who might attack you is only useful if it changes what you do. Start with the actors realistically interested in your organisation and look up the techniques they are known to use; MITRE ATT&CK groups and vendor threat reports list them. Then check whether your logging would see those techniques and whether your controls would stop them. That gap list is a far better security roadmap than a generic top-ten.

Capability and motive also set expectations for incident response. A financially motivated ransomware crew wants a quick payout and will move from access to encryption in days. A state-sponsored group may stay hidden for months, so finding one implant should start a hunt for others rather than end with re-imaging one machine.

cy-malware.heading: Defending against malware in layers
body: No single control stops malware, so defences cover each stage. Before execution: email filtering, blocking macros from the internet, application allowlisting, and patching browsers and document readers. During execution: EDR that watches behaviour such as Office spawning PowerShell or mass file renames, and attack surface reduction rules. After execution: network egress filtering to break command and control, and least privilege so a compromised user cannot reach everything.

Recovery is part of the defence. Offline or immutable backups that are tested regularly turn ransomware from an existential event into an expensive one. Combine that with an incident plan that says who isolates hosts and who decides on rebuilds, and the organisation can respond in hours instead of improvising for days.

cy-vulns.heading: Finding vulnerabilities before attackers do
body: Different techniques find different flaws. Static analysis (SAST) reads source code for patterns such as unsanitised input reaching a query. Dynamic testing (DAST) attacks the running application from outside. Software composition analysis checks third-party libraries against known CVEs, which matters because most application code today is open-source dependencies. Fuzzing feeds malformed input to find crashes that often signal memory-safety bugs.

None of these replaces design review. Threat modelling, for example with STRIDE, asks what could go wrong before code exists and catches whole classes of problems, such as a missing authorisation check on an API, that scanners struggle to see. Use the cheap automated checks on every commit and save manual review and penetration testing for the highest-risk components.

cy-cloud-arch.heading: Common cloud misconfigurations
body: Most cloud breaches come from configuration, not from attacks on the provider. The recurring mistakes are storage buckets or blobs left public, overly broad IAM permissions such as wildcard actions or unused admin roles, long-lived access keys committed to code, security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0 on management ports, and logging that was never enabled, so there is no record when something goes wrong.

The fixes are mostly guardrails rather than heroics: block public access at the account level, enforce least privilege with policies reviewed by tools such as IAM Access Analyzer, use roles and short-lived credentials instead of keys, scan infrastructure-as-code before deployment, and run continuous posture checks (CSPM) that alert when a resource drifts from the baseline.

cy-net-arch.heading: Verifying that segmentation works
body: A segmentation diagram is a claim; testing turns it into evidence. From a host in each zone, try to reach the services that the design says must be blocked, for example the database port from the user VLAN, and confirm the connection fails and the firewall logs the denial. Tools such as nmap from inside each segment, or automated breach-and-attack simulation, make this repeatable.

Re-test after changes. Rules accumulate over time: a temporary 'any-any' added for a migration, an over-broad object group, a forgotten VPN route. A regular rule review that removes unused and shadowed rules, combined with change control that requires a business owner for each rule, keeps the segmentation the design intended.

cy-secure-proto.heading: Checking a TLS configuration
body: Good protocol choice is easy to undermine with weak settings, so test what a server actually offers. `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -tls1_1` should fail on a modern server, and tools such as testssl.sh or the Qualys SSL Labs test list supported protocol versions, cipher suites, certificate chain problems and missing HSTS.

A sound baseline today is TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only, forward-secret key exchange (ECDHE), AEAD ciphers such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, a complete certificate chain, certificates renewed automatically before expiry, and HSTS on web services. Disable older protocols such as SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0 and 1.1 everywhere, including on internal services that are easy to forget.

secplus-concepts-scenarios.heading: Reading a concepts scenario
body: Concept questions in scenario form usually hide the principle behind a business story. A hospital wants doctors to see records only while treating a patient: that is least privilege with context, often attribute-based access control. A payment needs two people to approve: separation of duties. A guard checks badges and a camera records the door: a preventive control backed by a detective one.

Work out which principle the story is testing before reading the options. Then eliminate answers that are true statements but solve a different problem. When two options both fit, prefer the one that addresses the root cause, such as removing standing access, over one that only detects misuse afterwards.

secplus-crypto-scenarios.heading: Common cryptography traps in scenarios
body: Several distractors appear again and again. Hashing is not encryption: you cannot recover data from a hash, so 'hash the credit card numbers so support can read them' is wrong. Encoding such as Base64 provides no confidentiality at all. Encrypting with your private key does not keep a message secret; it proves authorship, which is what a signature does.

Also watch for key handling. Storing the encryption key next to the encrypted data, hard-coding it in source, or using one key for every customer defeats strong algorithms. The better answer usually involves a key management service or HSM, separate keys per purpose, rotation, and access to keys logged and restricted.

secplus-risk-scenarios.heading: A worked risk decision
body: A laptop fleet of 500 devices loses about 10 laptops a year. Each lost laptop with unencrypted data could cost $40,000 in breach notification and response, so the single loss expectancy is $40,000, the annualised rate of occurrence is 10, and the annualised loss expectancy is $400,000. Full-disk encryption costs $15,000 a year in licences and support and reduces the expected breach cost of a lost laptop to near zero.

The control is clearly justified: it removes most of a $400,000 expected annual loss for $15,000. The residual risk is the hardware cost and the small chance a laptop is stolen while unlocked, which management can accept and record. Scenario questions reward exactly this chain: compute ALE, compare it with the control cost, then name the response.

secplus-governance-scenarios.heading: Evidence that satisfies an auditor
body: Auditors test whether a control operated, not whether a document describes it. A password policy is a design; a configuration export showing the enforced settings, plus a sample of accounts tested against it, is evidence. An access review policy is a design; signed review records for each quarter, with removed accounts traced to tickets, are evidence.

Good evidence is dated, complete for the period, produced by the system rather than typed by hand, and traceable to the control it supports. Scenario answers that offer 'show the auditor the policy' or 'have the manager confirm verbally' are weak; answers that produce system-generated records for the audit period are strong.

secplus-thirdparty-scenarios.heading: Monitoring a vendor after onboarding
body: Risk does not end when the contract is signed. Vendors change ownership, move data to new subprocessors, suffer breaches, or let their certifications lapse. Ongoing monitoring means collecting each year's SOC 2 report and reading its exceptions, tracking the vendor's breach notifications and security ratings, and re-assessing when the scope of the service grows.

Tier vendors by risk so the effort matches the exposure. A vendor holding customer personal data or with network access deserves annual review and contract rights to audit; a vendor supplying office furniture does not. Keep the inventory current: an unknown vendor with an API key into production is a common finding after an incident.

cl-billing-support.heading: Support plans and when to use them
body: Cloud providers sell tiers of support. Basic support covers billing questions and documentation. Developer-level plans add technical help during business hours. Business or production plans add 24/7 support with faster response times for production-down cases. Enterprise plans add a named technical account manager and architecture reviews. Pricing is usually a percentage of the monthly bill with a minimum, so check the provider's current page.

Choose the tier by the impact of an outage, not by habit. A hobby project needs only basic support; a revenue-producing system usually justifies a plan with a one-hour response for production-impacting cases. Whatever the tier, use the provider's health dashboard and service quotas page first: many 'outages' turn out to be a quota limit that you can raise yourself.

awss-iam-foundations.heading: Finding and removing excess permissions
body: Least privilege is usually reached by trimming, not by perfect first drafts. IAM Access Analyzer reports resources shared outside your account or organisation and can generate a policy based on the actions a role actually used in CloudTrail. The IAM console's last-accessed information shows services a user or role has not touched in months, which are candidates for removal.

Credential hygiene matters as much as policies. Use the credential report to find access keys older than 90 days, keys never used, and users without MFA. Replace human IAM users with IAM Identity Center and federated sign-in, replace application keys with roles, and keep the root user locked away with hardware MFA and no access keys.

awss-incident-response.heading: Preparing before an incident
body: Most of incident response happens before the incident. Set up a dedicated security tooling account with cross-account roles that responders can assume, with permissions agreed in advance. Pre-create an isolation security group with no rules in each VPC, enable CloudTrail organisation-wide, GuardDuty and Security Hub in every Region, and store logs in a separate archive account.

Write and test playbooks for the likely cases: exposed access keys, a compromised EC2 instance, a public S3 bucket, and suspicious root activity. Run game days in a sandbox account so responders practise taking snapshots, isolating instances and revoking sessions. AWS's own incident response guide recommends exactly this preparation, because a team learning the console during an incident loses hours.

awss-monitor-analyze.heading: Querying logs with Athena and CloudWatch Logs Insights
body: Raw logs are only useful if you can ask them questions quickly. CloudWatch Logs Insights runs queries over log groups, for example counting `AccessDenied` errors by principal over the last hour. For long-term CloudTrail and VPC Flow Log data stored in S3, Amazon Athena queries the files in place with SQL, and partitioning by date and Region keeps queries fast and cheap.

A typical investigation query finds every API call made with a suspicious access key: filter CloudTrail on `userIdentity.accessKeyId`, sort by `eventTime`, and list `eventName`, `sourceIPAddress` and `errorCode`. Saving such queries as part of a playbook means the next responder starts with answers, not syntax.

awss-network-security.heading: Inspecting and logging traffic
body: Filtering decides what is allowed; inspection and logging tell you what actually happened. VPC Flow Logs record accepted and rejected connections at the network-interface level (addresses, ports, bytes, action) but not packet contents. AWS Network Firewall adds stateful inspection, domain filtering and Suricata-compatible IPS rules for traffic between VPCs or to the internet.

Traffic Mirroring copies packets from an instance's network interface to a monitoring appliance when full packet capture is needed. Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall blocks lookups of known malicious domains, which stops a lot of command-and-control traffic before a connection is made. Send these logs to the central archive and alert on rejects from internal sources, which often indicate scanning.

awss-iam-advanced.heading: Attribute-based access control with tags
body: As accounts grow, writing a policy per team does not scale. Attribute-based access control (ABAC) uses tags: a principal tagged `project=atlas` may act on resources tagged `project=atlas`, using a condition such as `"StringEquals": {"aws:ResourceTag/project": "${aws:PrincipalTag/project}"}`. New resources and people get access by being tagged correctly, without policy edits.

ABAC only works if tags are trustworthy. Restrict who can change tags with `aws:TagKeys` and `aws:RequestTag` conditions, enforce required tags with tag policies and SCPs, and pass identity-provider attributes as session tags at sign-in. Otherwise a user who can retag a resource can grant themselves access to it.

awss-data-protection.heading: Protecting data from deletion and ransomware
body: Encryption protects confidentiality; availability needs separate controls. S3 Versioning keeps prior versions of overwritten or deleted objects, and S3 Object Lock in compliance mode prevents anyone, including the root user, from deleting a version until its retention date. MFA Delete adds a second factor for permanent deletions.

For backups across services, AWS Backup with a vault lock makes recovery points immutable, and copying backups to a separate account means an attacker who compromises production credentials cannot also delete the backups. Also monitor KMS: scheduled key deletion has a waiting period of 7 to 30 days precisely so an alarm on `ScheduleKeyDeletion` gives you time to cancel a malicious or mistaken request.

awss-secure-compute.heading: Hardening container and serverless workloads
body: For containers, scan images in Amazon ECR (Inspector integrates with it), use minimal base images, run as a non-root user and set the root filesystem read-only where the app allows. Give each ECS task or EKS pod its own IAM role (task roles, or EKS Pod Identity / IRSA) instead of sharing the node's role, so one compromised container does not inherit every permission on the host.

For Lambda, give each function its own narrowly scoped execution role, keep secrets in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store rather than plain environment variables, set reserved concurrency to limit abuse, and enable code signing so only approved deployment packages run. Inspector also scans Lambda functions for vulnerable dependencies.

awss-governance.heading: Proving compliance continuously
body: Auditors increasingly expect evidence over a period, not a snapshot. AWS Audit Manager maps controls from frameworks such as CIS, PCI DSS or SOC 2 to automated evidence collected from Config, CloudTrail and Security Hub, and assembles assessment reports. AWS Artifact provides AWS's own compliance reports, such as its SOC reports and certifications, for the provider's half of the shared model.

Security Hub's security standards give a running score per account and control, which works well as a governance metric when tracked over time. Pair it with automatic remediation for low-risk, high-volume findings (for example, enabling S3 Block Public Access) and with exceptions documented in a register that has owners and expiry dates.

cissp-cap-d1.heading: How to approach a D1 scenario
body: Domain 1 questions place you in a governance role and ask what to do first, best or next. The answer is rarely a technical fix. Ask whose decision it is: senior management owns risk acceptance and policy approval, the data owner owns classification, and the security professional advises and implements. An option where the security team accepts risk on the business's behalf is usually wrong.

Next, look for the process step the scenario skipped. If a new regulation applies, a gap assessment comes before buying tools. If a control cannot be applied, a documented exception with compensating controls and an expiry comes before simply ignoring the requirement. Due care means acting as a prudent person would; due diligence means verifying that it actually happened.
Finally, remember the order of priorities that runs through the whole exam: people's safety first, then legal and regulatory obligations, then business objectives, then technology preferences.

cissp-cap-d2.heading: How to approach a D2 scenario
body: Asset security questions turn on who decides and what the data's classification requires. The data owner, a business manager, classifies data and approves access; the custodian, usually IT, implements the controls; users follow the handling rules. When an option asks the custodian to decide classification, or lets a user choose how to handle restricted data, it is usually a distractor.

Follow the data through its lifecycle: creation, storage, use, sharing, archiving and destruction. Most scenarios break one link. Production personal data copied into a test environment breaks 'use' and needs masking or synthetic data. A drive leaving the organisation breaks 'destruction' and needs purging or physical destruction appropriate to the media. A legal hold overrides normal retention and deletion schedules until counsel releases it.
When in doubt, choose the answer that reduces the amount of sensitive data held, because data you do not keep cannot leak.

cissp-cap-d3.heading: How to approach a D3 scenario
body: Security architecture questions reward principles over products. Look for which design principle the scenario violates: least privilege, defence in depth, fail-safe defaults, separation of duties, economy of mechanism, complete mediation or open design. The right answer usually restores the principle rather than adding a single new tool.

Cryptography scenarios in this domain are mostly about key management. Strong algorithms do not help if the key sits beside the data, never rotates, or is shared across all customers. Prefer answers that move keys into an HSM or key management service, separate duties between key administrators and data users, and plan for algorithm change (crypto agility), including the move to post-quantum algorithms such as ML-KEM.
For physical design questions, life safety outranks asset protection: doors on an escape route fail safe (unlock) on power loss even when that is less secure.

cissp-cap-d4.heading: How to approach a D4 scenario
body: Network security scenarios ask you to protect traffic and limit where an attacker can go. Start by identifying what crosses an untrusted network; that traffic needs encryption and authentication, such as IPsec between sites or TLS for applications. Then look at trust boundaries: guests, contractors, IoT devices and operational technology belong in their own segments with default-deny rules between them and the corporate network.

Many distractors add monitoring where prevention is possible, or add a device without addressing the design. An IDS that alerts on lateral movement is useful, but segmenting the flat network removes the path. A VPN does not help if the remote laptop is already compromised, which is why zero trust checks device posture and identity for every request.
Know the protocols' weaknesses too: Telnet, FTP and SNMPv1 send credentials in clear text, so the best answer replaces them with SSH, SFTP and SNMPv3 rather than merely monitoring them.

cissp-cap-d5.heading: How to approach a D5 scenario
body: Identity questions follow the account lifecycle: provisioning, review, change and removal. Many problems come from the middle of it. People change roles and keep old permissions (privilege creep), so the fix is periodic access reviews by the data owner and role-based provisioning tied to HR events. Leavers keep access because deprovisioning is manual, so the fix is automated removal on the termination record.

Prefer federation and single sign-on over shared or duplicated credentials, and phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys) over codes that can be relayed. Remember that authentication is only half the job: session tokens, API keys and service accounts are also credentials, so short session lifetimes, re-authentication for sensitive actions, and vaulted, rotated service credentials appear in many correct answers.

Accountability needs unique IDs. A shared administrator account cannot show who made a change, so replacing it with named accounts and privileged access management is almost always better than adding logging to the shared account.

cissp-cap-d6.heading: How to approach a D6 scenario
body: Assessment questions ask you to match the test to the question being asked. Vulnerability scanning finds known weaknesses broadly; penetration testing proves whether they can be exploited and chained; code review and SAST find flaws before release; a SOC 2 or ISO 27001 audit gives independent assurance about a vendor's controls. Choose the option that answers the scenario's actual question at the right depth.

Testing must be authorised. Before any penetration test, written rules of engagement must define scope, timing, methods and emergency contacts, signed by someone with authority over the systems. An option that starts testing on a verbal request, or tests a third party's systems without their consent, is wrong however efficient it sounds.
Results only matter when they reach decision-makers. Findings should be ranked by risk to the business, assigned owners and dates, reported in management terms, and re-tested after remediation.

cissp-cap-d7.heading: How to approach a D7 scenario
body: Operations scenarios often describe an incident in progress and ask for the next step. Use the incident response sequence: detect and analyse, then contain, then eradicate, then recover, then learn. If the attack is active, containment comes before investigation is finished; if it is contained, preserving evidence comes before rebuilding systems. Recovery before eradication invites the attacker back.

Evidence handling has firm rules: collect in order of volatility, work on verified copies (hash before and after), and keep a chain of custody for anything that may go to court. Notify according to the plan; legal counsel and management decide on external notification, not the analyst on shift.

For continuity questions, the priority is people's safety, then restoring the most critical business functions in the order set by the business impact analysis, not the order in which IT happens to find them.

cissp-cap-d8.heading: How to approach a D8 scenario
body: Software security questions reward building security in early. A flaw found in requirements or design costs far less to fix than one found in production, so answers that add threat modelling, secure coding standards and automated testing in the pipeline usually beat answers that rely on a final penetration test.

Third-party code is part of your software. Maintain a software bill of materials, scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities, pin and verify versions, and evaluate a new library's maintenance and licence before adopting it. For acquired software or SaaS, ask for evidence such as security test results or an attestation rather than a vendor's assurance.

When something goes wrong, contain first: a leaked secret is revoked and rotated before the history is cleaned, and a vulnerable release is patched or rolled back before the root cause analysis is written.
